attribution.note: Marcus's own tweet, embedded in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: The proposition matches his words. But target_version 'Muse Spark 1.2' is the drafter's inference, not Marcus's words; the dated Meta launch record points to Muse Glimmer instead. That target is not reliable.

contract.note: Marcus named no standard. Using the OSI AI Definition fits his stated concern about training data and transparency, so it is a fair, ordinary reading. Requiring the full NYT article, not just a headline in quotation marks, is also fair.

evidence.note: Meta's own dated announcement says the weights can be downloaded and calls it an open-weights model. This supports the open-weight part. It does not show what training materials were left out.
Reference standard requiring data information and training code. It defines the test but says nothing about this release.
Preserves the Aug 10 NYT headline with 'Open Source' in quotation marks. This backs the headline wording only; the quotation marks may be a qualification, and the article body is unverified.

reviews.rationale: Meta's disclosure supports the open-weight part. No dated release inventory shows the model failing the open-source standard. The NYT part rests on a headline in quotation marks, and the article itself was inaccessible, so the contract's requirement on the coverage is not met. The evidence does not settle the claim as a whole.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post.

semantics.note: Keeps 'often' and 'a lot of'. Drops 'really' and 'despite the hype', which are minor. The context ties the claim to withheld training data, and the contract restores that link.

contract.note: The plain reading (substantial classes of tasks blocked, not all tasks) is ordinary and fair, and it correctly refuses to invent a threshold for 'often'. The terms remain vague, so breadth has to be shown.

evidence.note: 2025 AISI abstract saying open weights allow more open research. It is outside the target period and does not address access to training data.
2024 study showing outsiders can analyse contamination. This is indirect, not inspection of the corpus, and it predates the target date.
Meta's own training summary for one release shows partial disclosure about processing. It is not a corpus or pipeline, and covers only one model.

reviews.rationale: No evidence shows, across open-weight releases in August 2026, how often missing data or training procedures blocked the specified tasks. The items are older or cover a single release. They neither establish nor refute the breadth the claim asserts.
